title: The Pacific Islands return to the International Comparison Program after 15 years: Why does it matter?
gist: Seventeen Pacific Island economies are rejoining the International Comparison Program after last participating in 2011, restoring directly measured Purchasing Power Parities that underpin global poverty, SDG and living-standards statistics; benchmark PPPs are targeted for publication in mid-2027.

insights.claim: Seventeen Pacific Island economies are returning to the International Comparison Program after last participating in 2011, restoring directly measured Purchasing Power Parities for the region.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A 15-year data gap in a whole region is being closed, improving the reliability of global poverty and living-standards comparisons that depend on PPPs.
insights.quote: 17 Pacific Islands’ economies are once again coming together to participate in the International Comparison Program (ICP)

insights.claim: The International Comparison Program produces Purchasing Power Parities that compare what people can buy across countries by accounting for price differences rather than exchange rates, compiling data from more than 175 countries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: PPPs, not exchange rates, are the backbone of cross-country welfare comparison, so gaps in coverage distort global aggregates.
insights.locator: The ICP produces Purchasing Power Parities

insights.claim: Since 2011 PPPs for these Pacific economies have been extrapolated from available economic data, but their reliability declines the longer time passes without a direct-data benchmark.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Extrapolated statistics degrade over time, making periodic direct benchmarks essential for accurate poverty and GDP figures.
insights.quote: While these extrapolations can provide reasonable short-term estimates, their reliability declines as more time passes

insights.claim: Purchasing Power Parities underpin Sustainable Development Goals monitoring, global poverty measurement, and indicators used by the World Bank Group, IMF, and United Nations.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Because PPPs feed the core global development metrics, their quality directly affects how poverty and progress are officially reported.
insights.quote: They underpin Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) monitoring, global poverty measurement, and a wide range of applications and indicators

insights.claim: Papua New Guinea and French Polynesia are more than 4,200 miles apart, farther than Miami to Anchorage, and many Pacific economies have populations below 400,000, with Tokelau and Niue under 2,000 residents.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Extreme dispersion and tiny populations make survey-based price collection costly, explaining why the region had dropped out of the program.
insights.quote: Papua New Guinea and French Polynesia are more than 4,200 miles apart - farther than the distance between Miami, Florida, and Anchorage, Alaska.

insights.claim: The Pacific Community adopted the World Bank's Survey Solutions software and built a tailored CAPI questionnaire for ICP price surveys, deploying a field-ready solution by August 2025 within a few months.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Digital survey tooling with built-in quality controls lowers the cost and error rate of statistical capacity building in remote regions.
insights.quote: resulting in a field-ready solution by August 2025

insights.claim: The Survey Solutions platform offers applications beyond the ICP, including Consumer Price Index data collection, by providing standardized data structures and built-in quality controls that reduce data-entry errors.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: One-time investment in digital survey infrastructure yields reusable capacity across a country's whole statistical system.

insights.claim: Pacific survey price data was collected from August through December 2025 with a validation workshop in April 2026, targeting publication of benchmark PPPs in mid-2027 as part of the next ICP global release.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Analysts relying on Pacific PPP data should expect refreshed direct benchmarks in the 2027 ICP release, superseding years of extrapolation.
insights.quote: the publication of benchmark PPPs for Pacific Island economies in mid-2027, as part of the next ICP global release.
insights.locator: The successful example of the Pacific Islands

insights.claim: The Pacific return was led by the Pacific Community in partnership with the World Bank and Asian Development Bank, financed through IDA under the PACSTAT project.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Multilateral financing and coordination were the enabling condition, illustrating the funding model for restoring statistical capacity in small states.
insights.locator: The Pacific Islands last participated in the ICP in 2011
